data: Status: the parser (M1) is released in v0.2.0, the lowering (M2) and the type system of core in v0.3.0; the rest is planned. This page is the design the bibliography recommends. Where the bibliography says a point is unmeasured, this page says so. The lowering section below records what was built.
data.base-run-it-unchanged#Base: run it uncha: Base is bootstrapped by evaluating base/boot.jl and then the file list of base/Base_compiler.jl and base/Base.jl. The recommendation is to run Base unchanged through the interpreter, at build time, and ship the resulting heap as an image. Only two things are ported to Go: the builtins, intrinsics and foreigncall targets; and hot leaf methods after profiling, replaced by method overrides registered in Go (same signature, same results, a test comparing both). Base is 140 705 lines whose semantics are the definition of Julia: a native rewrite would diverge, and every Base fix upstream would have to be ported twice.
data.lowering-the-design-as-planned-julialowe: src/julia-syntax.scm (+ macroexpand.scm, ast.scm) JuliaLowering/src language femtolisp Scheme, pattern-matching macros Julia, plain functions over a SyntaxGraph size 5 779 + 733 + 568 lines 13 940 lines status default in the system image but off by default provenance line numbers only byte-precise The recommendation is to port JuliaLowering: it is Julia with explicit data structures, closer to Go than Scheme pattern rewriting; it is MIT; it carries the provenance a notebook needs for file:line errors; and upstream is moving to it. The risk is that its coverage is not measured: if it lowers much less than Base, M2 becomes a port of julia-syntax.scm. The oracle in all cases is Meta.lower on the reference binary, compared on CodeInfo after renumbering slots and SSA values.
data.lowering-what-v030-built-m2#Lowering: wh:
The risk below came true in the sense the bibliography allowed: julia 1.12.6 lowers with the femtolisp front end by default and JuliaLowering is not part of the reference’s Meta.lower, so M2 is a port of julia-syntax.scm, the code that produces the goldens. The lower package ports julia-syntax.scm, macroexpand.scm, ast.scm and match.scm, pass by pass: expand-forms, resolve-scopes, analyze-variables!, closure-convert, linearize, then renumbering into CodeInfo. Hygiene (resolve-expansion-vars, rename-symbolic-labels) is ported too.
lower.NewState().Lower(ex) is Meta.lower of a macro-expanded top-level form: an Expr(:thunk, CodeInfo), an atom, or Expr(:error); one State per module, in file order. Macro expansion runs user code, so it stays with the caller, as in julia. Outputs are compared with julia’s field by field, modulo gensym numbering (the counters live for a whole julia session, so two sessions differ).
measured on forms identical to julia corpus (share/julia: base, Compiler, stdlib, test), 1191 files 53 997 53 997 (1191/1191 files) lowering snippets 124 124 macro-made toplevels still in hygienic scopes 48 48 built expressions (error paths, rare heads) 477 477 deparse vs julia --lisp 119 119 front-end functions vs julia --lisp 151 151 Statement coverage is 100%, every expectation coming from julia. Lower refuses trees deeper than lower.MaxDepth (1000) with lower.ErrLimit, and FuzzLower runs on every pull request. Known gap: a Float64 inside a lowering error message makes Lower return lower.ErrUnsupported.
data.parser-port-juliasyntax#Parser: port Jul: JuliaSyntax is the default parser since Julia 1.10, and Base itself loads it. Bootstrapping forces a native parser. Until Base loads it, Julia parses base/*.jl with the femtolisp parser in C. A Go VM has no femtolisp, so it needs a Go parser before any Julia runs; running JuliaSyntax through the interpreter is not an option for the first files. JuliaSyntax is a hand-written recursive-descent parser over a token stream with a separate green tree, and a module that builds Expr. It ports line by line to Go, as rbgo’s parser was built. Oracle: the real JuliaSyntax.parseall(Expr, …) on every file of base/, stdlib/, test/ and the JuliaSyntax test corpus, compared as serialised Expr trees.
data.parser-usage-v020#Parser: usage (v0.2.0):
syntax.ParseAll(src, filename) in go-embedded-julia/julia returns the same Expr as julia’s Meta.parseall, including julia’s error Expr: the statements before the first error, then Expr(:error) or Expr(:incomplete) with the formatted ParseError.
e := syntax.ParseAll([]byte("f(x) = x^2 + 1"), "cell.jl") serialises to
(:toplevel {L 1 :"cell.jl"} (:"=" (:call :f :x) (:block {L 1 :"cell.jl"} (:call :"+" (:call :"^" :x 2) 1)))) Parsing is bounded (64 MiB, depth 4000) and ParseAllLimits returns an error rather than an Expr on failure. Known gap: on a few malformed inputs JuliaSyntax itself throws and julia falls back to femtolisp, which is not ported; there ParseAll returns Expr(:error) and ParseAllLimits an error wrapping syntax.ErrParserFailed.
data.released-m3-julias-base-runs-v0130#Relea:
The interpreter runs julia 1.12.6’s real Base and its seven stdlibs (FileWatching, Libdl, Artifacts, SHA, Sockets, LinearAlgebra, Random). sysimg.jl builds the whole system image; VM.RunModuleInitializers runs Base.__init__ and every stdlib’s __init__. 16 Base-level task programs (@async, Channel, Condition, Timer, sleep, ReentrantLock, Threads.@spawn, ScopedValue) give julia’s own text/plain output.
Tasks and the event loop (interp/taskswitch.go, taskget.go, uvloop.go, cfunction.go). A task is a goroutine and a baton channel says whose turn it is, so exactly one goroutine runs julia code at any time. jl_new_task, jl_switch, _start_task and jl_finish_task are ported from task.c, and the per-task VM state (world age, call depth, exception stack, typeinf timing, finalizers inhibited) is saved and loaded at each switch. jl_task_get_next is scheduler.c’s for one thread: when no task is runnable, the libuv loop, written in Go (async and timer handles, uv_ref/uv_unref, jl_close_uv, jl_process_events), runs once. @cfunction evaluates to a Ptr{Cvoid} that holds the callable and its signature, which the loop calls. The thread calls answer as julia -t 1 does. VM.MaxTasks and VM.MaxHandles bound the tasks and handles, and a task that waits when nothing can wake it is refused with ErrDeadlock naming the waiting task, where julia would sleep for ever (a stated divergence). Call VM.Close when the VM is done, to end the goroutines of tasks left waiting.
The VFS has two modes (interp/vfs.go), one layer under every file call Base makes. In the sandbox, the default, only julia’s own tree exists (the Base sources and the stdlibs, embedded unmodified), read-only, and no path leaves it. With VM.Host set, the tree stays mounted at its paths and every other path is the real file system, on macOS, Linux and Windows. Reading is ported; writing a file is refused in the sandbox (EROFS) and is not ported on the host yet (#32).
Dynamic libraries (interp/dlload.go) are the libraries the interpreter implements in Go (GMP, MPFR, PCRE2 and dSFMT so far, and the libraries the JLLs open). dlopen finds them by julia 1.12.6’s file names, and any other library cannot be opened, in the sandbox or on the host: loading a C library is a stated divergence. libblastrampoline reports julia’s configuration. A library that is open but whose functions are not written yet (OpenBLAS: from v0.18.0 gemm, gemv and the level-1 routines, and from v0.22.0 the level-3 trsm, trmm, syrk and symm, in single and double precision, are forwarded to go-blas; LAPACK, #67) refuses each call as not ported, never silently.
Also new: a module reference names the module object, not its name, and runtime calls such as uv_random, llvmcall of atomics.jl’s IR templates and jl_module_names are ported. The package builds on every Go target and is tested on 386, arm, riscv64, s390x, ppc64le and loong64 (floats are bit-exact independently of the FPU), on macOS, Linux and Windows.
Known limits: [@async i^2 for i in 1:4] is correct but takes minutes, which is under investigation; the stdlibs are still julia’s .jl sources, and rewriting them in Go is #36; BLAS has gemm, gemv and level 1 only since v0.18.0, and trsm, trmm, syrk and symm since v0.22.0, while LAPACK (lu, qr, \ on a general matrix, eigen, svd) and UpperTriangular(A) \ B are still refused (#67); writing a file in host mode is not ported yet (#32). The statements about “Not yet: Base” in the v0.6.0 to v0.12.0 paragraph above are the state of those releases.
data.released-so-far-the-core-package-v030#Re:
core — Julia’s type objects, apply_type, and subtyping (a port of jltypes.c and subtype.c of 1.12.6, without intersection): identical to julia on 20 000 random pairs and 4 902 cases from test/subtype.jl.
FuzzSubtype runs on every pull request. Subtyping is 1.37× slower than julia’s jl_subtype on one core (3.26 ms against 2.39 ms for the 20 000 pairs, best of 7 interleaved rounds, load 4.4–6.6, 2026-11-01), an open defect: #20. It was 1.43× before the query environments were pooled (v0.9.1), which halved the allocations (−51%, −66% of bytes); the time gain of the pooling alone is not confirmed at low load.
data.released-so-far-the-interp-package-v060-: interp — a port of julia 1.12.6’s src/interpreter.c that runs lowered code over Core. interp.New().NewSession().Eval(src) parses, lowers and runs a cell; interp.Repr shows the value as julia does. struct and abstract type definitions (v0.7.0) run through the builtins lowering calls, which build the default outer and inner constructors as jl_ctor_def does; calling a type dispatches on its constructors, and user-defined outer constructors join them. Methods with where clauses (v0.8.0) dispatch with static parameters (e.g. f(x::T) where {T<:Integer} = T), through the TypeVar and UnionAll constructors of boot.jl:335-338, built in Go until boot.jl runs. Structs and abstract types with parameters (v0.9.0): Q(1) infers Q{Int64}, Q{Integer}(1) runs the inner constructor, a parameter no field constrains gets no outer constructor (as jl_ctor_def decides), constructor signatures keep the called type first as in julia’s one method table, and a type argument dispatches as Type{X}. Macros are expanded before lowering (v0.10.0), a port of jl_expand_macros: a macro call runs the macro’s method with __source__ and __module__, hygiene goes through the hygienic-scope that lower resolves, nested and recursive calls are expanded in turn, quotes go through lower.Backquote, and a self-expanding macro raises StackOverflowError. Boot (v0.11.0): Core is defined by julia 1.12.6’s own base/boot.jl, unmodified and embedded; vm.Boot() evaluates all 363 forms in Core, then runs post_boot_hooks (jltypes.c:3909-3968), so builtins raise boot.jl’s exception types and an error in an included file is a LoadError. After Boot, vm.CoreSession().Eval(src) runs code in Core; Boot is opt-in and interp.New().NewSession().Eval is unchanged. Ported from julia’s C sources for it: the types jl_init_types creates (real layouts for the IR nodes, GenericMemory, GenericMemoryRef and Array, plus AddrSpace and Core.CPU), module expressions with relative using .M / import ..M paths, the builtins _primitivetype, setfield!, invokelatest and invoke_in_world, getfield of types and AST nodes, the intrinsics trunc_int, sext_int, zext_int, bitcast, shl_int, lshr_int and ashr_int, and ccall to Go shims keyed by the C function’s name (an unknown name is ErrUnsupported when the call runs). include reads only VM.Sources, never the host’s filesystem, and an include that nests without end raises StackOverflowError. Arrays (v0.12.0) are julia 1.11+’s: GenericMemory and GenericMemoryRef values with the builtins memorynew, memoryrefnew, memoryrefoffset, memoryrefget, memoryrefset! and memoryref_isassigned (builtins.c:1711-1856, genericmemory.c) with julia’s checks and messages; Array{T,N}(undef, dims…) builds as boot.jl does, with the overflow-checked intrinsics checked_[su]{add,sub,mul}_int. Values show as julia 1.12.6 shows them (Int8[1, 2], Any[#undef, 1, #undef], [1 2 3; 4 5 6], Matrix{Int64}(undef, 0, 3), Vector{Int64}, Matrix{T} where T<:Integer); only the array and memory aliases are matched (julia’s general alias search needs type intersection), and a MemoryRef shows its index where julia shows an address. An Expr’s args is one Vector{Any} per expression (ex.args === ex.args); writes, a new memory or size, and setfield! of head/args reach what lowering reads, and an Expr is shown as Expr(:call, :f, 2) until julia’s quoted show is ported. a = 1; b = 2 on one line now expands and lowers each form. VM.MaxMemoryElems (16 Mi elements by default) bounds one allocation with interp.ErrMemoryLimit; the total a VM allocates is not bounded yet (#24). Speed is not measured: there is no julia counterpart until programs index arrays through Base. Not yet: atomic memory, and Base. Boot has no julia counterpart to measure against, since julia’s Core comes from its system image. Core has the built-in types, the exception and AST types of boot.jl and jltypes.c (with the QuoteNode, LineNumberNode and Expr constructors), 26 builtins and the integer and float intrinsics. 97 Core-only programs show the same value in Go and julia 1.12.6; 100% statement coverage; fuzzed (FuzzEval). Not yet: Base (+, println, a.b, constructor arguments that need convert, macros that use esc or Base’s macros), splatting anything but a tuple or a simple vector (it calls Base.iterate), redefining a struct that has parameters (it needs Base.getproperty), const and atomic fields, arrays, finally; the speed against julia’s interpreter is not measured yet.
data.risks-the-plan-names#Risks the plan name: Subtyping and specificity diverging silently from subtype.c. JuliaLowering’s coverage of Base, not yet measured. Interpretive speed: Base’s generic code relies on inlining and specialisation. Mitigations are dispatch caches keyed by concrete argument types, fast paths for intrinsic-only methods, and Go overrides for measured hot leaves. Pointers and unsafe_*: a pointer must be modelled as a buffer and an offset into Go memory, checked on every access, so that a malformed unsafe_load raises instead of corrupting the VM. Security: notebook and playground cells are untrusted. The plan fuzzes the parser and the image reader, and bounds recursion depth, allocation sizes and regex steps. Unicode version must match utf8proc’s, or test/unicode.jl diverges. Upstream moves fast: the sources were read at 1.15.0-DEV; the plan pins a release and tracks the next one deliberately.
data.runtime-in-go#Runtime in Go: C file (lines) Go component jltypes.c 4 728, datatype.c 3 200 type objects: DataType, UnionAll, Union, TypeVar, Vararg, layout, type cache; field layout must match for sizeof, fieldoffset, reinterpret subtype.c 7 737 issubtype, type_intersection, morespecific: the hardest part, with test/subtype.jl (3 666 lines) and test/specificity.jl as oracles gf.c 6 567, typemap.c 1 795, method.c 1 538 method tables, dispatch cache, world ages, ambiguity builtins.c 3 161 the builtins (63 in julia 1.12.6; 83 on 1.15-DEV, where the line counts were taken), each a Go function runtime_intrinsics.c 1 862 the intrinsics (93 in julia 1.12.6; 94 on 1.15-DEV, where the line counts were taken) interpreter.c 1 118, toplevel.c 1 020 the interpreter over CodeInfo and top-level eval module.c 2 504 modules, bindings, binding partitions genericmemory.c 631, array.c 324 Memory{T} and MemoryRef; Array is defined in Julia on top task.c, partr.c, gc-*.c, signals-*.c a goroutine per Task with a hand-off channel (one runs at a time, as in Julia’s single-threaded scheduler); the Go GC; no signals staticdata.c 5 103 the interpreter’s own image format; not a port of sys.ji subtype.c is where a reimplementation diverges silently (the diagonal rule, Union distribution, Vararg, TypeVar bounds). The plan is to port it statement by statement rather than from the paper.
data.the-image-is-the-start-up#The image is t:
Julia without a system image evaluates boot.jl and all of Base at start. Through an interpreter that is 140 705 lines, plus the 36 867-line Compiler if inference is interpreted: minutes, not seconds. So the build runs the bootstrap once, natively, and writes the resulting heap (modules, bindings, types, method tables, lowered CodeInfo, interned symbols, the _return_type cache, constant data such as Unicode tables) to a versioned binary image, embedded with go:embed or fetched next to the WebAssembly module. This is Julia’s own design (sys.ji) without native code.
The image size is unknown until M4. The start-up budget to hold is that image deserialisation stays under the Ruby core’s 2.3 s on the same machine (a figure the plan reports but did not re-measure); per-module images (LinearAlgebra only when using LinearAlgebra runs) are the lever if it is not met.
data.the-interpreter#The interpreter: Its shape follows JuliaInterpreter: a Frame with locals (slots) and SSA values, a program counter over CodeInfo.code, GotoNode, GotoIfNot and ReturnNode as control flow, and :enter and :leave as an exception-handler stack. JuliaInterpreter is the evidence that lowered IR is directly executable for the whole of Base. Its limit is also the port’s: it hands foreigncall and llvmcall to compiled wrappers, which is exactly where the Go port needs its shim table instead.
data.the-notebook-bridge#The notebook bridge: The Ruby cells of go-notebook define the contract to copy: one shared interpreter for all cells of the language; only variables cross; a cell defines the top-level names it assigns and uses the names it reads first, taken from the language’s own parser; errors are reported at the notebook line. The plan proposes a Julia to Go value table (integers at their width, BigInt as *big.Int, BigFloat as *big.Float, String as string, arrays as *ndarray.Array sharing the same buffer with column-major strides kept) and a go-scikit/julia package modelled on go-scikit/ruby. Julia is column-major and go-ndarray is NumPy-style strided, so go-ndarray must accept Fortran strides without copying: the plan lists that as unconfirmed.
data.the-pipeline#The pipeline: source ──JuliaSyntax (Go port)──▶ Expr ──macroexpand──▶ Expr ──JuliaLowering (Go port)──▶ CodeInfo ──▶ toplevel eval (toplevel.c semantics) ──▶ method tables ──call──▶ dispatch (gf.c, typemap.c, subtype.c) ──▶ interpreter over lowered IR (interpreter.c semantics) ──▶ builtins (63 in julia 1.12.6), intrinsics (93 in julia 1.12.6), foreigncall shim table This is the pipeline Julia’s own developer documentation describes (eval.md), minus the code-generation step. Julia already interprets some top-level code instead of compiling it, and “the bulk of the work to interpret code is handled by eval in interpreter.c”. The port makes the interpreted branch the only one.
data.type-inference-only-where-bases-results-:
Base calls inference for results, not only for speed: Base._return_type is used by promote_op, and through it by map, broadcast and collect on empty inputs and by accumulate. map(x -> x + 1, Int[]) returning Vector{Int} and not Vector{Any} is an observable result. Two options:
interpret Compiler/src (36 867 lines) itself, lazily, only when _return_type is called: correct by construction, slow; a small Go abstract interpreter over the same lowered IR: fast, and wrong in the corners. The recommendation is option 1 first, with a per-signature cache that is part of the image; option 2 only if measurement shows the notebook waiting on it, and then checked against option 1.
data.what-julia-is-made-of#What Julia is made: Part Path Lines Role for a Go port C/C++ runtime and codegen src/*.{c,cpp,h} 169 453 a specification; the LLVM half is dropped its semantic core subtype.c, gf.c, jltypes.c, datatype.c, builtins.c, module.c, … (15 files) 36 477 what must be re-expressed in Go Base, in Julia base/**/*.jl (202 files) 140 705 run as is through the interpreter type inference and optimiser Compiler/src (41 files) 36 867 not needed for speed; see below parser, in Julia JuliaSyntax/src (18 files) 11 326 port to Go lowering, in Julia JuliaLowering/src (17 files) 13 940 port to Go legacy front end, femtolisp src/*.scm (11 files) 10 622 oracle and fallback JuliaInterpreter src/*.jl (12 files) 6 943 design reference test suite test/**/*.jl (297 files) 130 413 oracle The lowered IR has 12 node types and 30 Expr heads: that is the whole instruction set an interpreter must execute. Julia’s own C interpreter over it is 1 118 lines.

data: Status: released in v0.14.0 (the image) and v0.15.0 (Kernel); current in v0.24.0, with soft scope, julia’s MethodError text, Get, Set, Has, TypeOf, a Reset that stops the tasks and timers cells started, an empty catch_backtrace() (v0.23.0) and a Base image that carries the inference of a Float64 matrix display (v0.24.0). This page is the usage of the package interp for a notebook: how a VM starts in about a second instead of building Base for 13 minutes, and how a cell runs on it. The README of the repository holds the same flow in brief.
data.cancellation-and-budgets#Cancellation an:
Cancelling ctx raises InterruptException in the running cell (Eval answers ErrCellCanceled, wrapping ctx.Err()). The interrupt is delivered once at first, so that a finally or a wait list cleans up, and again until the cell ends, so that a catch cannot swallow it. A cell that waits (sleep) is woken. Per-cell budgets, on the kernel or per EvalWith:
Field Bound Error Timeout wall time of the cell, its display included (30 s by default) ErrCellTimeout MaxSteps statements executed ErrStepLimit MaxAlloc elements the cell’s allocations take in total (2^25 by default) ErrMemoryLimit MaxOutput bytes of each of stdout and stderr (1 MiB); the rest is dropped Result.Truncated A zero field is the kernel’s value, a negative one means no bound.
data.eval#Eval:
r := k.Eval(ctx, `f(x) = x + 1; f(41)`) // r.Value "42" julia's text/plain display of the last value // r.Stdout, r.Stderr what this cell printed, apart from every other cell's // r.Err nil, a *JuliaError (type and showerror's text), or a typed error A cell that throws is a value, and the next cell runs. A cell defines names in Main; functions, structs and redefined methods persist from cell to cell.
The text of an error is julia’s own showerror, MethodError included (the “Closest candidates” list, the ambiguity and its proposed fix, the keyword and world-age hints), compared character for character with julia 1.12.6 on the cases the test suite lists.
Soft scope. Cells run as the REPL and IJulia run them (REPL.softscope): a loop or a block at the top of a cell assigns to a global that exists instead of making a local, so s = 0 in one cell and for i in 1:10; s += i; end in the next gives s == 55. CellOptions{HardScope: true} gives the scope of a file (include_string) instead.
data.go-values-in-and-out-get-and-set#Go valu:
k.Get(name) reads a global of Main as a Go value and k.Set(name, v) assigns one, as a cell name = v would, also over an existing binding. Both copy, never alias, and are refused with ErrKernelBusy while a cell runs.
julia Go Int64 int64 (Set also takes an int) Float64 float64, every bit kept: NaN payloads, -0.0 Bool, String bool, string Vector{Float64}, Vector{Int64} []float64, []int64 Matrix{Float64}, Matrix{Int64} interp.Matrix[float64], interp.Matrix[int64]: Rows, Cols, Data column-major, At(i, j) k.Set("v", []float64{1, 2, 3.5}) k.Eval(ctx, "w = v .* 2") w, ok, err := k.Get("w") // []float64{2, 4, 7} Get answers (value, ok, err): ok is false for a name that is not bound; a value of any other type is a *ConversionError (errors.Is(err, ErrKernelType)) that names the julia type, and Set of a Go type outside the table names the Go type. A name that is no identifier is ErrKernelName, and an array over VM.MaxMemoryElems is ErrMemoryLimit. Set checks a slice’s length (and a Matrix’s Rows*Cols, overflow-checked, against len(Data)) against VM.MaxMemoryElems before it converts anything, so a refused slice costs a few KiB. A matrix with a zero dimension reads back with its shape, whichever dimension is the zero.
k.Has(name) answers whether a global of Main is bound, and k.TypeOf(name) julia’s type of it as text (Matrix{Float64}), also for a type the table does not convert; neither copies the value. Both return an error, not a bare false, while a cell runs: (false, ErrKernelBusy) is not the answer “no”.
data.known-limits#Known limits: Backtraces are off, as in a julia run with them off (v0.23.0): catch_backtrace() and the backtrace of a failed task are empty, and jl_get_excstack answers an empty vector, instead of failing as not ported. The first Float64 matrix product and its display on a fresh kernel take 0.84 million interpreter statements, where they took 69.6 million (v0.24.0): the display calls Base._return_type, which runs julia’s own compiler in the interpreter, and the image builder now runs the display of a Float64 matrix before it saves, so the inferred code is in the image. The first display of another element type may still pay that cost. BLAS computes gemm, trsm, trmm, syrk and symm, gemv and the level-1 routines for Float64 and Float32 (A * B, A * x, x' * y, A' * A, Symmetric(A) * B, UpperTriangular(A) * B, B / UpperTriangular(A)), through go-blas (v0.3.0 for level 3), within its stated error bound of the exact value and not bit for bit with OpenBLAS. The complex types and LAPACK (A \ b of a general A, lu, qr, eigen, svd) fail until go-blas has them, and so does UpperTriangular(A) \ B, which julia sends to LAPACK’s trtrs, not to trsm (#67). A Memory of Float64 is stored as a []float64 (v0.21.0): the double-precision routines read and write it in place, at 1.02 to 1.16 times the cost of calling go-blas directly (3 to 22 times when the elements were boxed), and Kernel.Get and Set of a []float64 or a Matrix[float64] box nothing. The price is on the read: an interpreted Float64 loop boxes one more allocation per element (s += v[i] over 10^6 elements: +2.70% allocations, sum(v) +1.13%, v .+ 1.0 +0.52%). A Memory of Float32 is still boxed, so a single-precision call copies the elements it reads and writes. rand(m, n) reaches an llvmcall that is not ported (#120). The first matrix display of an element type other than Float64 may still pay the cost of inference that the Float64 one no longer does (see above). A VM without Base (Boot() only) shows values and errors as the Go repr and cells use Core’s names. The image is not authenticated by itself (#49): pin the digest. Cold start measured on darwin/arm64 (Apple M4 Max): load plus kernel about 1 s, the first cell under a millisecond; the load alone is about 0.65 s.
data.reset#Reset:
info, err := k.Reset() // info.Reloaded the image was loaded again (the log was past its bound) // info.Undone the writes replayed; info.Tables the method tables reverted Reset puts the kernel back in the state NewKernel returned it in, for the next run of a notebook: what the cells defined, assigned, imported, overloaded or mutated is gone, the generator behind rand included, and the next cell runs as the first of a fresh kernel. It is refused with ErrKernelBusy while a cell runs.
It costs what the cells changed, not the size of the image. Every write to an object the image holds (setfield!, swapfield!, modifyfield!, replacefield!, setfieldonce!, memory stores and copies) is logged with the value it replaces, and Reset replays the log in reverse; the methods of the functions a cell defined into or deleted from are reverted to the world of the start, and the bindings, usings and options of every module are put back. An object a cell made carries no log. Measured on a corpus of 18 cells (definitions and redefinitions, a struct, a show overload on it, an overload of a Base method, using LinearAlgebra, seeded rand, a push! to Base.LOAD_PATH, a delete_method of a Base method, a module, errors), which wrote 3790 times to objects of the image: Reset took 0.6 ms, loading the image again about 0.85 s. The same corpus runs on a kernel after a Reset as on a fresh one, cell for cell (TestKernelResetBase).
The bound. The log holds DefaultMaxUndo (262144) entries, about 18 MiB. Past it, Reset loads the image again into a new VM and says so (ResetInfo.Reloaded; k.VM() is another VM then, with Stdout, Stderr, MaxSteps, MaxDepth and MaxMemoryElems carried over). A kernel made by NewKernel from a VM, not from an image (LoadKernel and FetchKernel keep the image’s bytes for the reload), has nothing to load: Reset answers ErrResetOverflow and changes nothing.
Tasks and timers (v0.20.0). Before it rolls back, Reset stops the tasks a cell started that have not finished and closes the libuv timers it opened (ResetInfo.Tasks, ResetInfo.Timers; k.Tasks() counts them for an embedder), so that the replay restores the lists such a task waited in without it. A stopped task never runs again, and none of its finally or catch blocks runs: user code during a Reset could print, block or write the state the Reset is restoring. The task’s object is marked done, so istaskdone and wait answer as for a task that ended. A timer is dropped as close(t) would be, without its close callback. Base’s own tasks are left alone. A kernel also yields once when it is made, so that the tasks Base makes in its initializers are parked before the state Reset returns to.
What Reset does not undo, by design:
Go-side state a cell reaches through a ccall: open files and sockets, the environment, the working directory, what was already written to Stdout and Stderr, the clock, libraries opened with dlopen, the state of libgmp and libmpfr. The caches. A type a cell made stays in the weak type caches of the image’s types until the collector drops it, and method specializations and compiled bodies stay. A limit an embedder set through k.VM() is the one in force. The world counter and the object-id counters, which only move forward: Base.get_world_counter() and objectid of a new object differ from a fresh kernel’s. A write from Go code to a field of the image that is the interpreter’s own bookkeeping (method-instance and code-instance caches, task state). A cell’s own writes are all logged. An unseeded rand() differs from one fresh kernel to the next, since the generator is seeded when the kernel starts. After a Reset the generator is in the state it started in, so the first draws are the ones the kernel would have made first (TestKernelResetRNG).
data.sandbox#Sandbox: The sandbox is the default: the file system is julia’s own tree and the environment is empty. Host mode is KernelOptions{Host: true}, never a default, and a VM that is already in host mode is refused without it (ErrKernelHost). There is one kernel per VM and one running cell per kernel (ErrKernelExists, ErrKernelBusy). Two kernels in one process share core’s type tables, which are guarded, and the hints an image sets on core’s shared types; an image sets them once and another image may not change them, so kernels over images of one release are safe and a second release is refused at its load. Since v0.20.0 a load writes nothing to the boot types its VM put in those shared caches (a refused load leaves them as they were), and since v0.21.0 New may be called from several goroutines at once.
data.the-image-and-why-a-digest-is-pinned#The:
Each release of julia publishes its system image as the asset julia-image-vX.Y.Z.bin, with julia-image-vX.Y.Z.sha256. The release workflow builds it from the tag, and the bytes are the same on linux/amd64, linux/arm64 and darwin/arm64. The digest of a version cannot be written in that version’s own source, since the image depends on the source; so, as go.sum does, the consumer pins it. images.sum at the root of the repository lists the digest of each release.
An image is not authenticated by its key or its trailer, and loading one writes state the whole process shares (issue 49 of the repository). Nothing reaches LoadImage that does not have the pinned digest:
digest, err := interp.ParseDigest("a4568120…") // from images.sum or the release notes k, err := interp.FetchKernel(ctx, "v0.15.0", digest, interp.FetchOptions{}, interp.LoadOptions{}, interp.KernelOptions{}) if err != nil { … } defer k.Close() FetchKernel is FetchImage, then LoadImage, then NewKernel. FetchImage downloads over https within a size bound (256 MiB by default), refuses any other digest with ErrImageDigest before the bytes are decoded, keeps the verified file in the user cache directory and hashes it again at every use. A program that ships the image itself uses LoadKernel(reader, …) or NewKernel(vm, …) on a VM it loaded.
LoadOptions.Digest. A program that holds the image bytes pins the digest at the load: LoadOptions{Digest: &digest} makes LoadImage and LoadKernel hash the whole input first and refuse any other bytes with ErrImageDigest, before the key, the framing or any object is looked at. The field is a pointer, so that unset (the image is not pinned) cannot be a pinned all-zero digest by accident. Load an image from an untrusted source with its digest. A load is atomic with respect to what the process shares: the types and hints an image adds are committed in one step after every conflict has been looked for, and a refused image (ErrImageConflict) changes none of them.

data: Status: planned. No code has been translated yet. This page records what the plan allows, and the rules it will hold to.
data.inside-base-with-their-own-licence#Insid: base/ryu/* is under the Boost licence, and base/special/rem_pio2.jl and base/special/hyperbolic.jl carry an FDLIBM notice. Both run as Julia through the interpreter, and the notices travel with the image.
data.libraries-base-calls-replaced-not-linked: Library Licence What the plan does GMP LGPL-3.0-or-later or GPL-2.0-or-later not linked, not translated: replaced by math/big and go-bignum, written from the documented semantics, not from its source MPFR LGPL-3.0-or-later the same PCRE BSD-3-Clause replaced by a front end on go-ruby-regexp utf8proc MIT replaced by Go’s unicode and x/text/unicode/norm libuv MIT replaced by Go’s os, net and time OpenBLAS and LAPACK BSD-3-Clause replaced by go-ndarray’s linalg
data.the-gpl-parts-to-avoid#The GPL parts to:
SuiteSparse’s libumfpack, libspqr and librbio are GPL-2.0-or-later, and libcholmod is LGPL-2.1-or-later and GPL-2.0-or-later. They back SparseArrays, an external standard library, whose \ on sparse matrices goes to UMFPACK and CHOLMOD. A Go port of SparseArrays must use the fleet’s sparse solvers (go-sparse) and must not read SuiteSparse source. Julia’s stock build includes these libraries (USE_GPL_LIBS ?= 1 in Make.inc), so they are a thing to keep out, not a thing that is absent.
FFTW is GPL but is not in Julia’s tree: FFTW.jl is a registry package, and the plan serves its API over go-fft instead.
data.what-may-be-translated-to-go-with-the-no:
Julia is MIT, and Julia’s THIRDPARTY.md states that the language “consists of the compiler (the contents of src/), most of the standard library (base/ and stdlib/)”. So these are all MIT and may be translated to Go with the notice kept:
Source Licence src/ (the C runtime) MIT base/, stdlib/ MIT JuliaSyntax/ MIT JuliaLowering/ MIT JuliaInterpreter.jl MIT LinearAlgebra.jl, Statistics.jl MIT src/flisp (femtolisp) BSD-3-Clause dSFMT BSD-3-Clause; may be translated

data:
Status: in development. M0 (oracle harness), M1 (parser), M2 (lowering) and M3 (runtime) are done, released as v0.2.0 (M1), v0.3.0 (M2) and v0.13.0 (2026-11-14, M3) of go-embedded-julia/julia, against julia 1.12.6. The current release is v0.24.0: M4’s image and M6’s per-cell Eval, value table and Reset (which stops the tasks and timers cells started) are in it, and BLAS computes for gemm, trsm, trmm, syrk, symm, gemv and the level-1 routines, in place on a typed Float64 store (the rows below say what is left). M4 to M7 are not finished.
M3 in numbers: v0.13.0 runs julia 1.12.6’s real Base and its seven stdlibs (FileWatching, Libdl, Artifacts, SHA, Sockets, LinearAlgebra, Random). sysimg.jl builds the whole system image, VM.RunModuleInitializers runs Base.__init__ and every stdlib’s __init__, and 16 Base-level task programs (@async, Channel, Condition, Timer, sleep, ReentrantLock, Threads.@spawn, ScopedValue) give julia’s own text/plain output. Tasks run on goroutines over a libuv loop written in Go; the VFS has a read-only sandbox mode and a host mode; dynamic libraries are the ones implemented in Go, and loading a C library is a stated divergence. Known limits: [@async i^2 for i in 1:4] is correct but takes minutes (under investigation); the stdlibs are still julia’s .jl sources (rewriting them in Go is #36); BLAS had no kernel at v0.13.0, and from v0.18.0 it has gemm, gemv and level 1, and from v0.22.0 trsm, trmm, syrk and symm, with LAPACK (lu, qr, \ on a general matrix, eigen, svd) and UpperTriangular(A) \ B still to come (#67); writing a file in host mode is not ported yet (#32). The detail is in Architecture.
M2 in numbers: the lower package ports julia 1.12.6’s femtolisp front end (julia-syntax.scm, macroexpand.scm, ast.scm, match.scm). lower.NewState().Lower(ex) is Meta.lower of a macro-expanded top-level form, compared with julia field by field, modulo gensym numbering. It is identical on 53 997 of 53 997 forms of julia 1.12.6’s share/julia tree (base, Compiler, stdlib, test; 1191 of 1191 files), 124 of 124 lowering snippets, 48 of 48 hygienic-scope forms and 477 of 477 built expressions (error paths, rare heads); deparse matches julia --lisp on 119 of 119 forms and the front-end functions on 151 of 151 calls. Statement coverage is 100%. Lower refuses trees deeper than lower.MaxDepth (1000) and FuzzLower runs on every pull request. Known gap: a Float64 inside a lowering error message makes Lower return lower.ErrUnsupported.
M3, release by release before v0.13.0: core — Julia’s type objects, apply_type, and subtyping (a port of jltypes.c and subtype.c of 1.12.6, without intersection): identical to julia on 20 000 random pairs and 4 902 cases from test/subtype.jl; and method specificity (jl_type_morespecific, v0.4.0), identical to Base.morespecific on the same corpus. core/dispatch (v0.5.0): method tables with world ages, and the method a call with concrete argument types runs, with its static parameters: identical to julia’s which and dispatch environment on 9 000 calls over 1 500 random method tables (4 675 method choices, 1 968 with static parameters, 87 ambiguities). interp (v0.6.0 to v0.12.0): a port of julia 1.12.6’s src/interpreter.c that runs lowered code over Core (interp.New().NewSession().Eval(src), interp.Repr); v0.7.0 runs struct and abstract type definitions with julia’s default constructors (jl_ctor_def) and user-defined outer constructors, and calling a type dispatches on its constructors. v0.8.0 dispatches methods with where clauses with static parameters (e.g. f(x::T) where {T<:Integer} = T), through the TypeVar and UnionAll constructors of boot.jl:335-338, built in Go until boot.jl runs. v0.9.0 runs structs and abstract types with parameters (struct Q{T}, abstract type A{T}): Q(1) infers Q{Int64}, Q{Integer}(1) runs the inner constructor, a parameter no field constrains gets no outer constructor (as jl_ctor_def decides), constructor signatures keep the called type first as in julia’s one method table, and a type argument dispatches as Type{X}. v0.10.0 expands macros, a port of jl_expand_macros: a macro call runs the macro’s method with __source__ and __module__, hygiene goes through the hygienic-scope that lower resolves, nested and recursive macro calls are expanded in turn, quotes go through lower.Backquote, and a self-expanding macro raises StackOverflowError. v0.11.0 defines Core by julia 1.12.6’s own base/boot.jl, unmodified and embedded: vm.Boot() evaluates its 363 forms in Core, then runs post_boot_hooks (jltypes.c:3909-3968), so builtins raise boot.jl’s exception types and an error in an included file is a LoadError. After Boot, vm.CoreSession().Eval(src) runs code in Core; Boot is opt-in, and interp.New().NewSession().Eval is unchanged. Ported from julia’s C sources for it: the types jl_init_types creates (with real layouts for the IR nodes, GenericMemory, GenericMemoryRef and Array, plus AddrSpace and Core.CPU); module expressions and relative using .M / import ..M paths; the builtins _primitivetype, setfield!, invokelatest and invoke_in_world; getfield of types (DataType, TypeName, TypeVar, UnionAll, Union, Vararg) and of AST nodes; the intrinsics trunc_int, sext_int, zext_int, bitcast, shl_int, lshr_int and ashr_int; and ccall to Go shims keyed by the C function’s name (an unknown name is ErrUnsupported when the call runs). Display fixes, checked against julia 1.12.6: Float32 (1.0f0, NaN32), Char (escapes, malformed bytes, \u/\U) and nested modules (Main.L.B). include reads only VM.Sources (julia’s embedded sources by default), never the host’s filesystem, and an include that nests without end raises StackOverflowError. v0.12.0 runs julia 1.11+’s arrays: GenericMemory and GenericMemoryRef values with the builtins memorynew, memoryrefnew, memoryrefoffset, memoryrefget, memoryrefset! and memoryref_isassigned (builtins.c:1711-1856, genericmemory.c), Array{T,N}(undef, dims…) as boot.jl builds it, the overflow-checked intrinsics checked_[su]{add,sub,mul}_int, arrays and where-clause types shown as julia 1.12.6 shows them, and an Expr’s args as one Vector{Any}; VM.MaxMemoryElems bounds one allocation (interp.ErrMemoryLimit), the total is not bounded yet (#24). Not yet: atomic memory, and Base. Speed of arrays: not measured, there is no julia counterpart until programs index arrays through Base. Speed: Boot has no julia counterpart to measure against, since julia’s Core comes from its system image. Core has the built-in types, the exception and AST types of boot.jl and jltypes.c (with the QuoteNode, LineNumberNode and Expr constructors), 26 builtins (the six type-definition builtins and fieldtype are new in v0.7.0, _typevar in v0.8.0, _expr and _apply_iterate in v0.10.0) and the integer and float intrinsics. Checked: 97 Core-only programs show the same value in Go and julia 1.12.6; 100% statement coverage; fuzzed (FuzzEval). Not yet: type intersection, and with it the interference sets julia 1.12 uses to order matches; Base (+, println, a.b, and constructor arguments that need convert, macros that use esc or Base’s macros), splatting anything but a tuple or a simple vector (it calls Base.iterate), redefining a struct that has parameters (it needs Base.getproperty), const and atomic fields, arrays, finally, and the remaining builtins and intrinsics. Speed: subtyping is 1.37× slower than julia’s jl_subtype on one core (3.26 ms against 2.39 ms for the 20 000 pairs, best of 7 interleaved rounds, load 4.4–6.6, 2026-11-01), an open defect (#20); pooling the query environments (v0.9.1) halved the allocations (−51%); the speed of the interpreter against julia’s is not measured yet.
M1 in numbers: a Go port of JuliaSyntax 29ec5226f7b1, the version julia 1.12.6 ships. Tokens, green trees and Expr are identical to julia’s on 1191 of 1191 files of julia 1.12.6’s share/julia tree (base, Compiler, stdlib, test; 18.5 MB) and on 976 of 976 golden snippets. On one core the corpus parses in 0.98 s against 1.39 s for julia’s Meta.parseall (0.70x). Parsing is bounded (64 MiB, depth 4000) and fuzzed; coverage is 100%, tested natively on amd64/arm64/386, under qemu on riscv64/loong64/ppc64le/s390x/arm, compiled for every GOOS/GOARCH, and run on wasip1 under wazero. Known gap: on a few malformed inputs (import. .., import. ...x, 0:0:<) JuliaSyntax itself throws and julia falls back to the femtolisp parser, which is not ported: there ParseAll returns Expr(:error) and ParseAllLimits returns an error wrapping syntax.ErrParserFailed.
Effort is on the roadmap’s scale: S days, M weeks, L months, XL several months. M3 and M4 dominate; in total the effort is on the order of the rbgo effort, plus a parser and a lowering pass that rbgo did not need in this form.
data.how-conformance-is-measured#How conforma:
Julia’s test suite is written with the Test standard library, and test/choosetests.jl lists the test names. The harness:
runs each listed file under the reference julia and under the interpreter, one file per worker process with a timeout, each with a Test reporter that emits one JSON record per @test (file, line, expression, pass, fail, error or broken); compares records, not totals: a test passing in both, failing only in the interpreter (a defect), or failing in both (upstream), so that an equal count with different members is not read as parity; keeps a committed allowlist of files out of scope (precompile, loading, llvmcall*, threads, ccall to user libraries, spawn, cmdlineargs, compiler, jit), each with a reason, and reports the pass rate per remaining file; stores every failure found only in the interpreter as a regression test once it is fixed. The differential oracles of each stage (M1 Expr, M2 CodeInfo, Random streams, printed show output) are stronger than the suite for the front end and are built first, which is why M0 comes before everything else.
data.milestones#Milestones: # Milestone State Contents Size Exit test M0 oracle harness done: v0.1.0 (2026-10-26), against julia 1.12.6; go run ./cmd/jloracle regen regenerates the goldens a Go tool that runs the reference julia (a pinned release) on a corpus and stores its outputs: parse trees, Meta.lower, Test summaries, printed values S outputs checked in as golden files, regenerated by one command M1 parser done: v0.2.0 (2026-10-26), 1191/1191 files and 976/976 snippets identical Go port of JuliaSyntax/src (11 326 lines) to a Go Expr; fuzzed (go test -fuzz) with a depth and size bound L Expr-identical on all 202 base/ files, stdlib/, all 297 test/ files, and JuliaSyntax’s own tests M2 lowering and macro expansion done: v0.3.0 (2026-10-28), 53 997/53 997 corpus forms (1191/1191 files) identical Go port of julia 1.12.6’s femtolisp front end (julia-syntax.scm, macroexpand.scm, ast.scm, match.scm) L CodeInfo-identical (modulo numbering) to Meta.lower on Base’s top-level forms M3 Core runtime done (v0.13.0: julia’s real Base and seven stdlibs run, with tasks, an event loop and a two-mode VFS): type objects, apply_type, subtyping (v0.3.0), specificity (v0.4.0), method tables and dispatch of concrete calls (v0.5.0), interpreter interp (v0.6.0), with struct and abstract type definitions (v0.7.0) methods with where clauses (v0.8.0), structs and abstract types with parameters (v0.9.0), macro expansion (v0.10.0), and Core defined by julia’s own boot.jl (vm.Boot, v0.11.0), and julia’s arrays (v0.12.0) types, subtyping, method tables, dispatch, the builtins (63 in julia 1.12.6), the intrinsics (93 in julia 1.12.6), the interpreter, boot.jl XL test/subtype.jl, test/specificity.jl, test/intrinsics.jl, and the parts of test/core.jl that need no Base I/O M4 Base bootstrap and image partial: the image is done (v0.14.0, see Kernel); the test/ list is planned Base_compiler.jl and Base.jl evaluated; the jl_*, libc and libuv shim (about 524 + 88 + 78 call sites); the Compiler interpreted for _return_type; an image writer and reader XL Base loads, and the test/ files arrayops, strings, dict, tuple, reduce, broadcast, iterators, sorting, numbers, int, math, float16, ryu, show M5 numeric boundary planned GMP and MPFR on math/big and go-bignum, a PCRE2 front end on go-ruby-regexp, utf8proc tables, a dSFMT port, Printf, Dates, Random, Statistics, LinearAlgebra on go-ndarray L test/gmp.jl, mpfr.jl, regex.jl, unicode.jl, rational.jl, complex.jl; the go-scikit bindings and the example notebook (the exit test) are planned the Julia to Go value table, the names a cell defines and uses, errors, worker limits M a mixed Go and Julia example notebook transcript in the go-notebook docs M7 WebAssembly playground planned a lazily loaded Julia core, image loading, SVG display through the existing sanitizer M first result under the Ruby core’s time on the same machine; data.scope-of-the-first-version#Scope of the:
In: all syntax JuliaSyntax parses; functions and multiple dispatch with parametric methods and where; keyword arguments; closures; struct and mutable struct; abstract and parametric types; Union, Nothing and Missing; tuples and named tuples; try/catch/finally; hygienic macros and @generated functions; string interpolation; broadcasting; comprehensions and generators; do blocks; modules; using and import of in-image modules; single-threaded tasks and Channel. From the standard library: LinearAlgebra (dense, over go-ndarray), Statistics, Random, Printf, Dates and Test. SparseArrays comes later.
Out: ccall to arbitrary user libraries (an error naming the symbol), llvmcall, @cfunction, parallel Threads.@threads (runs serially), Distributed, Pkg (packages ship in the image), and precompilation of user code.
data.what-the-playground-will-show#What the p:
Milestone by milestone, as the plan lists it:
Milestone The playground shows M1 parser a cell’s Expr tree (dump) and parse errors with JuliaSyntax’s diagnostics M2 lowering Meta.@lower of a cell: the CodeInfo listing M3 Core arithmetic, isa, typeof, <: queries, user-defined types and methods with dispatch, using Core only M4 Base println, strings, Vector/Dict/Set, comprehensions, broadcasting, sort, sum, BigInt factorials, r"…" matches, @show, @time (wall clock only) M5 numeric stdlib LinearAlgebra (A \ b, eigen, svd), Statistics (mean, std, quantile, cor), Random with seeds identical to julia’s output, Printf, Dates M6 bridge a mixed Go and Julia notebook; go-scikit bindings (Stats, Special, Plot SVG) There is no playground yet.

data: Status: M3 is done (v0.13.0); M4 and M5 are planned. This page counts what Julia’s Base asks of its runtime, and says which fleet library is meant to answer each part. As of v0.13.0, Base runs: the type system (core), the tasks and the libuv loop, the VFS and the dynamic libraries the VM implements in Go (GMP, MPFR, PCRE2 and dSFMT so far) are in place, and loading a C library is a stated divergence. Since v0.18.0 the BLAS routines gemm, gemv and level 1 (Float64, Float32) are forwarded to go-blas, and utf8proc is a Go port; since v0.21.0 a Memory{Float64} is a typed []float64 that the double-precision routines use in place, and since v0.22.0 the level-3 trsm, trmm, syrk and symm are forwarded too. Not yet: LAPACK (lu, qr, \ on a general matrix, eigen, svd) and UpperTriangular(A) \ B (#67), and the stdlibs rewritten in Go (#36).
data.builtins-63-in-julia-1126#Builtins: 63 i: julia 1.12.6 has 63 builtins; the bibliography counted 83 on julia 1.15-DEV sources. From src/builtin_proto.h: getfield, setfield!, isa, ===, <:, apply_type, _apply_iterate, invoke, memorynew, the twelve memoryref*, the fourteen *global*, _structtype, _typebody! and the rest. Each is one Go function.
data.ccall-and-ccall-in-base-896-call-sites-i:
856 ccall and 40 @ccall, plus 24 cglobal(. By target:
Target Sites Go implementation Julia runtime jl_*, ios_* 524 (387 unique names) is the Go runtime: reflection, IdDict, strings, files, GC; no-ops or errors for compiler, precompile and CPU-feature calls libc and OS symbols 88 Go os, syscall and time; memcpy and friends on Go slices; malloc and free on a Go arena MPFR 81 static, plus 29 generated go-bignum’s bigfloat and math/big.Float; mpfr_asprintf and mpfr_snprintf need a Go formatter libuv uv_* 78 Go os, os/exec, net and time.Timer; the event loop becomes goroutines that wake the scheduler GMP 40 named, plus 3 interpolated math/big.Int and big.Rat, following GMP’s truncating, floor and ceiling rounding for quotients; go-bignum for factorial and binomial other dynamic (pointer, @static, interpolated) 7 resolved case by case PCRE2 18 see Regex below utf8proc 15 Go unicode and golang.org/x/text/unicode/norm; width and grapheme tables generated from the Unicode version pinned by utf8proc Windows-only and macOS libproc 13 not on WebAssembly; GOOS=windows later libm 0 nothing: Base’s elementary functions are written in Julia over intrinsics, so results are bit-identical by construction The standard libraries read (Random, Dates, Printf, Statistics) have 14 sites: 7 on libdSFMT in Random (the MersenneTwister generator; the default Xoshiro is pure Julia), 3 on MPFR (mpfr_snprintf in Printf, two mpfr_sub_* in Random), 1 on libuv in Dates, and 1 on the runtime. Statistics has 0.
data.fft#FFT: Julia’s Base and standard library have no FFT (no FFTW in base/, stdlib/ or deps/; FFTW.jl is a registry package). A go-julia-fftw package presenting the FFTW.jl and AbstractFFTs.jl API over go-fft is the port, and it is not part of the VM.
data.intrinsics-93-in-julia-1126#Intrinsics::
julia 1.12.6, the release the port follows, has 93 intrinsics. The breakdown below is the bibliography’s, counted on julia 1.15-DEV sources, which have 94: 81 ADD_I, 12 ALIAS and 1 ADD_HIDDEN in src/intrinsics.h. By group (1.15-DEV):
Group Count wrap (bitcast) 1 arithmetic 17 fast arithmetic (aliases) 7 comparisons 15 bitwise 11 conversion 9 checked arithmetic 10 functions (abs_float, copysign_float, sqrt_llvm, …) 9 pointer arithmetic 2 pointer access 2 pointer atomics 6 C interface (cglobal, llvmcall) 2 CPU tests (have_fma, cpu_supports) 2 hidden (cglobal_auto) 1 All except llvmcall and the pointer group map to Go in a few lines each, with math/bits and math. Int128 needs a two-word type, and Float16 and BFloat16 are converted in software. muladd_float is computed as a fused multiply-add, and that choice is documented. pointerref, pointerset and the atomics work on the Go-side byte storage of Memory and Ref: there is no raw address space. llvmcall is not supported: Base has 0 llvmcall( sites.
data.linearalgebra-194-sites#LinearAlgebra: 1: 182 call BLAS or LAPACK through libblastrampoline, inside loops over element types (blas.jl 38, lapack.jl 144: 105 distinct callee expressions), 9 sites over 8 lbt_* names, and 3 sysctlbyname. The mapping is to implement the Fortran BLAS and LAPACK interface of each routine family as Go functions over go-ndarray’s linalg (LU, QR, Cholesky, SVD, Eig, Eigh and least squares exist there), on the column-major Memory{Float64} buffer a Julia Matrix owns, without copying. Families go-ndarray lacks (generalized Schur, banded and tridiagonal factorisations, Bunch-Kaufman) are missing kernels to add to go-ndarray, not to the VM. State at v0.24.0 (unchanged since v0.22.0): the BLAS routines gemm, gemv, the level-1 routines and trsm, trmm, syrk and symm are forwarded to go-blas, in place on a Memory{Float64} (a typed []float64 since v0.21.0, at 1.02 to 1.16 times the cost of calling go-blas directly); a Float32 memory is still boxed and copied. LAPACK is not forwarded yet (#67).
data.naming-of-the-packages-around-the-vm#Nam: The plan’s naming mirrors go-embedded-ruby: go-embedded-julia/julia for the VM, with docs, the landing and brand; go-julia- organisations for ports of Julia packages that are not part of the image’s standard library (FFTW, SparseArrays, DataFrames, Distributions, SpecialFunctions); and go-scikit/julia for the go-scikit bindings. A go-julia-* package is Julia code run by the VM plus Go kernels imported from the go-scikit libraries, never a second Go implementation of the same algorithm.
data.regex#Regex: base/regex.jl has PCRE2 semantics. The fleet’s engine is go-ruby-regexp, a pure-Go backtracking VM reimplementing Onigmo. PCRE2 and Onigmo differ in syntax corners (\K, (*VERB)s, callouts, variable-length lookbehind, \h, option letters). The plan is a PCRE2 syntax front end that compiles to the same VM, with test/regex.jl as the oracle and the 18 pcre2_* names implemented on it. If the VM cannot take a construct, the interpreter raises Julia’s ErrorException("PCRE compilation error: …") rather than match differently.
